books.section: Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

stimulus.source_note: Paraphrase of the account of the Panic of 1857 in Wikipedia, “Panic of 1857,” and civilwar.com, “The Crash of 1857,” consulted 2026-11-26. The Panic of 1857 is not covered in the three books’ Topic 5.6 sections; the facts here were verified against those two secondary sources. The wording is original.
stimulus.text: Paraphrase: In August 1857, the Ohio Life Insurance and Trust Company failed, and the panic spread fast: banks stopped paying out gold, railroad stocks fell, and more than 5,000 American businesses failed within a year. The North’s factories and railroads suffered most, while the South’s cotton trade stayed strong, and Southerners pointed to the panic as proof that their slave economy was sounder than Northern free labor.

source: original; stimulus as noted in stimulus.source_note
stem: Southerners who pointed to the panic as proof their economy was sounder were using it to argue that

options.text: slavery made the South stronger than free labor.
the North should adopt slavery as well.
options.misconception: Southerners praised slavery, they never asked the North to adopt it; their point was Southern strength.

options.text: Congress should raise the tariff at once.
options.misconception: Background from the books: the tariff of 1857 cut rates; the panic argument was about slavery, not the tariff.

options.text: banks should stop lending money to farmers.
options.misconception: The panic began with a bank failure, not farm lending; the argument was about slavery’s strength.

rationales.A: If the slave economy stood firm while free labor’s banks and railroads failed, Southerners said, slavery was the sounder system.
rationales.B: Southerners praised slavery, they never asked the North to adopt it; their point was Southern strength.
rationales.C: Background from the books: the tariff of 1857 cut rates; the panic argument was about slavery, not the tariff.
rationales.D: The panic began with a bank failure, not farm lending; the argument was about slavery’s strength.
rationales.general:
1. See the contrast: Northern banks and railroads failed while Southern cotton held.
2. Hear the Southern claim: their slave economy was sounder than Northern free labor.
3. See the sting: an economic argument became a defense of slavery itself.
4. Watch the politics: Southerners used the panic to argue that slavery, not free labor, was the sound economy.
Remember: when one section weathers a storm the other drowns in, the storm becomes evidence.
